title_en: 272: Space, The Final Investing Frontier -  How AI and Technology Are Expanding the Econom
title_zh: 太空，投资的最后前沿：AI 与科技如何拓展经济（Reid Menge，BlackRock）
subtitle_zh: BlackRock 的 Reid Menge 拆解入轨成本骤降如何催生太空数据中心与新一轮投资浪潮。
summary_zh: 本期 The Bid 由 Oscar Pulido 对话 BlackRock Fundamental Equity Group 投资组合经理 Reid Menge，把太空从科幻叙事拉到投资语境。Menge 认为真正的转折点是 SpaceX 那场 750 亿美元 IPO——首日市值达 1.7 万亿美元、开盘 150 美元、收盘略低于 161 美元——以及一个更根本的驱动：入轨成本曲线。历史上把一公斤有效载荷送入轨道要花约 54,000 美元，SpaceX 的 Falcon 9 已把它压到约 3,000 美元，而正在研制、比自由女神像还高约 100 英尺的完全可复用 Starship，则承诺把成本进一步降到约 200 美元/公斤——一旦到那个水平，会催生一整批新公司与子行业。他用两个 C 加一个 D（cost、capability、demand）作为分析框架：成本下降之外，卫星正从过去地球同步轨道（geo-orbit）上校车那么大、5 亿美元一颗的通信卫星，演化成烤面包机大小的低轨小卫星，Planet Labs 这类公司几乎每天把地球每一平方英寸都拍下来；再加上终端直连卫星（direct-to-device）的蜂窝通信，需求侧被彻底打开。Menge 特别强调 AI 与太空的交织：一座地面 AI 数据中心一吉瓦容量约需 400 亿到 500 亿美元投资，其中电力占约 200 亿美元，而太空中太阳能发电效率约为地球五倍，把算力放到轨道上主攻的正是这一块——这也是太空数据中心（space data center）概念的经济学起点。他还从地缘政治角度指出太空已成与陆地、海洋并列的争夺领域，并按镐头和铁锹（picks and shovels）梳理投资顺序：半导体、通信设备、激光器、火箭零部件、耐高温特种材料，再到地球观测、天气制图等二三阶服务。整体是一堂把入轨成本、AI 算力与国家安全三条线索打通的太空投资入门课。
description: 272: Space, The Final Investing Frontier -  How AI and Technology Are Expanding the Econom

turns.en: All systems check. Engines are green for ignition. Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, fire! For decades, space was largely associated with government programs, scientific exploration, and the occasional moonshot.
turns.zh: 各系统检查完毕。引擎绿灯，可以点火。十、九、八、七、六、五、四、三、二、一，点火！几十年来，太空在很大程度上是与政府项目、科学探索以及偶尔的登月壮举联系在一起的。

turns.en: But today, much of the global economy already relies on infrastructure in orbit, from communications and navigation to weather forecasting and the data that powers businesses around the world.
turns.zh: 但今天，全球经济的很大一部分其实已经依赖于在轨基础设施——从通信、导航到天气预报，再到为全球各地企业运营提供动力的数据。

turns.en: There's, as we speak, 30 U.S. government GPS satellites circling above us. We've gotten now down to the point where you can create a satellite the size of a toaster.
turns.zh: 就在我们说话的当下，有30颗美国政府的GPS卫星正在我们头顶环绕飞行。现在已经做到了可以造出一台烤面包机那么大的卫星。

turns.en: Now, a combination of technological advances, falling costs, growing private sector involvement, national security priorities, and the rise of artificial intelligence could be pushing the space economy into a new phase.
turns.zh: 而技术进步、成本下降、私营部门参与度提升、国家安全优先事项，以及人工智能的兴起，这一组合可能正在把太空经济推向一个新的阶段。

turns.en: So is space moving from something that feels futuristic to a much more tangible economic and investment theme? Welcome to The Bit, where we break down what's happening in the markets and explore the forces changing the economy and finance.
turns.zh: 那么，太空是否正在从一种听起来很科幻的感觉，转变为一个更切实的经济和投资主题？欢迎收听 The Bid，在这里我们把市场上正在发生的事情拆开讲清楚，也一起探索那些正在改变经济与金融的力量。

turns.en: I'm Oscar Polita. Today, I'm joined by Reid Mengi, portfolio manager in BlackRock's Fundamental Equity Group. We'll look at what's driving the growth of the space economy, how AI and national security are reshaping the industry, where economic opportunities may be emerging, and what investors should be watching as this market develops.
turns.zh: 我是 Oscar Pulido。今天和我坐在一起的，是 BlackRock 传统股票团队（Fundamental Equity Group）的组合经理 Reid Menge。我们来看一下是什么在推动太空经济的增长，AI 与国家安全如何重塑这个行业，哪些经济机会正在浮现，以及投资者在这个市场演进过程中应该关注什么。

turns.en: Reid, thank you so much for joining us on The Bit. Thanks, Oscar. Appreciate the opportunity. Well, Reid, we're here to talk about space and the space economy.
turns.zh: Reid，非常感谢你来到 The Bid。谢谢你，Oscar，很荣幸受邀。好，Reid，我们今天要聊的是太空和太空经济。

turns.en: Of course, when people think about space or hear about space, I think they think about things like rockets and astronauts and exploration. And I think about when I was in school, we used to go to the planetarium and we'd sit there and we'd look up at the stars and learn about astronomy.
turns.zh: 当然，人们一想到太空、一听到太空这个话题，想到的可能是火箭、宇航员、太空探索。我想起上学那会儿，我们常去天文馆，坐在那里抬头看星星、学天文学。

turns.en: But it turns out that space already plays a pretty significant role in our everyday lives from an economic perspective. So why don't we start there?
turns.zh: 但结果发现，太空其实从经济角度看，已经在我们的日常生活中扮演着相当重要的角色。那我们就从这里开始聊吧？

turns.en: What does the space economy actually look like today? And where are we already relying on it? That's right, Oscar. If you mention it to most people, they'll probably think of some of the greatest moments in American history, or they'll think about maybe a Ron Howard film.
turns.zh: 现在的太空经济到底长什么样？我们已经在哪些方面依赖它了？没错，Oscar。如果你跟大多数人提到这个词，他们多半会想到美国历史上一些最伟大的瞬间，或者想到一部 Ron Howard 的电影。

turns.en: You say there was space to an investor. You'd probably get a blank stare. The topic for investors, I would say, is relatively new. And really, that was SpaceX, the IPO this past summer, the spectacular IPO, which put it on the radar for investors.
turns.zh: 你要是对一个投资人说'太空'，他大概率会一脸茫然。对投资者来说，这个话题其实相当新。真正把它推到投资人雷达上的，是 SpaceX 在今年夏天那场轰动一时的 IPO。

turns.en: The Space and AI firm has officially made history on its $75 billion IPO, debuting with a market value of $1.7 trillion a head. SpaceX shares store in tonight what's been called Wall Street's biggest initial public offering of stock.
turns.zh: 这家太空+AI 公司在其 750 亿美元的 IPO 上正式书写了历史，上市首日市值一举达到 1.7 万亿美元——SpaceX 股票今晚迎来了被称为华尔街迄今最大规模的股票首次公开募股。

turns.en: Shares opened at $150 before finishing the day just below $161. But you ask a good question, you know, where is it today in your lives? And really, the answer is that it's everywhere.
turns.zh: 开盘报 150 美元，收盘略低于 161 美元。但你问了一个很好的问题——今天它到底在你生活里在哪儿？答案是：无处不在。

turns.en: From the government's perspective, space is heavily involved in U.S. defense, national security. There's, as we speak, 30 U.S. government GPS satellites circling above us.
turns.zh: 从政府的角度看，太空深度嵌入了美国的国防与国家安全。就在我们说话的当下，有 30 颗美国政府 GPS 卫星正在头顶环绕。

turns.en: They're doing more than just positioning planes and ships. They're also helping Uber figure out where you are and where your driver is. So there's a lot of commercial applications on top of just weather forecasting.
turns.zh: 它们可不只是在给飞机和轮船做定位，它们还在帮 Uber 判断你在哪儿、你的司机在哪儿。所以除了天气预报之外，还有大量的商业应用。

turns.en: Increasingly, we're seeing precision agriculture. And so space really is a very important topic that's emerging in both the government and in the civilian world as well.
turns.zh: 我们越来越多地看到精准农业（precision agriculture）。所以太空，无论是在政府侧还是民用世界，都是一个正在浮现的、极其重要的话题。

turns.en: And this is where you're seeing this emergence of the data center in space. So just framing it, space has been about exploration, national exploration.
turns.zh: 而这正是你看到'太空数据中心'这一概念浮现的地方。我们先给个框架：太空此前一直是关于探索、关于国家层面的探索。

turns.en: It's in the current stage of satellites. But what we're moving into is space being about the commercialization opportunities and data centers floating 15,000 miles above us in the not too distant future.
turns.zh: 现在处于卫星阶段。而我们正在走向的，是太空开始围绕商业化机会展开——在不太远的将来，数据中心会漂浮在我们头顶 15,000 英里的轨道上。

turns.en: So, Reed, you mentioned how space already has some relevance in our everyday lives. You mentioned satellites, and that's how we think about things like knowing what the weather is going to be like.
turns.zh: Reid，你刚才提到太空其实已经和我们日常生活有一些关联。你提到卫星，这也是我们理解诸如天气预报这类事情的方式。

turns.en: And there are governments that use it from a national defense perspective. So it's relevant. But why does it feel like space is having more of a moment right now?
turns.zh: 还有一些政府是从国防角度在用它。所以它确实有意义。但为什么现在会让人感觉太空正在迎来属于它的'时刻'？

turns.en: Why is it rising in importance? You mentioned SpaceX and the IPO, but maybe just elaborate. Why is it becoming more of a popular topic? Great question, Oscar.
turns.zh: 为什么它的重要性在上升？你提到了 SpaceX 和那场 IPO，可以再展开讲讲吗——为什么它正在变成一个更热门的话题？问得好，Oscar。

turns.en: It's two C's and a D, cost, capability, and demand. And we'll start with the cost piece. Historically, to get mass to orbit, it would cost about $54,000 per kilogram.
turns.zh: 是两个 C 加一个 D：成本（cost）、能力（capability）、需求（demand）。我们先说成本。历史上，把一公斤有效载荷送入轨道大概要花 54,000 美元。

turns.en: So when you see those NASA space shuttles, that's basically what it's costing to get a kilogram to orbit, about $54,000. And that was U.S. government for decades.
turns.zh: 所以你看到的那些 NASA 航天飞机，那时候把一公斤东西送上轨道的成本大概就是这个数——约 54,000 美元，而这个水平美国政府维持了几十年。

turns.en: You had the private sector for the past decade create a lot of innovations in this industry where SpaceX in particular with the Falcon 9 rocket has gotten that number from $54,000 down to about $3,000 per kilogram to orbit.
turns.zh: 过去十年，私营部门在这个行业做了很多创新，尤其是 SpaceX 的 Falcon 9 火箭，把数字从 54,000 美元一公斤压到了大约 3,000 美元一公斤入轨。

turns.en: The next step is going to be the Starship. This is the fully reusable rocket that SpaceX is working on. Starship is about 100 feet taller than the Statue of Liberty.
turns.zh: 下一步是 Starship。这是 SpaceX 正在研制的完全可复用火箭。Starship 比自由女神像还要高大约 100 英尺。

turns.en: It's absolutely enormous. The promise with Starship is getting that cost curve down even further, down from $3,000 per kilogram down to about $200.
turns.zh: 它巨大无比。Starship 带来的承诺，是把成本曲线进一步压低——从每公斤 3,000 美元降到大约 200 美元。

turns.en: At that point, you're going to be able to create all new companies, all new sub-industries of space, new opportunities. This topic is all about how cheaply can you get mass to orbit.
turns.zh: 到了那个水平，就能催生出一批全新的公司、全新的太空子行业、全新的机会。整个话题的核心就是：你能以多低的成本把质量送入轨道。

turns.en: The analogy, Oscar, would be if United Airlines had to throw away a plane every time it flew from San Francisco to New York, it'd be a very expensive plane ticket.
turns.zh: Oscar，打个比方：如果 United Airlines 每次从旧金山飞到纽约都得把飞机扔掉一次，那机票一定贵得离谱。

turns.en: So that's the goal of SpaceX, to really bring down the cost to get mass to orbit. And at the end of the day, that's the first piece we got to solve, the reusability of rockets.
turns.zh: 所以 SpaceX 的目标就是真正压低把质量送入轨道的成本。说到底，这是我们要解决的第一件事——火箭的可复用性。

turns.en: The second C is capability. And what I mean by that is the satellites are becoming much smaller, much cheaper than historically the world's ever seen.
turns.zh: 第二个 C 是能力。我指的是卫星正在变得比以前小得多、便宜得多，是这个世界前所未见的。

turns.en: So it used to be that a communication satellite that operated in the geo-orbit would cost about $500 million be the size of a school bus and weigh as much as an elephant.
turns.zh: 过去，一颗运行在地球同步轨道（geo-orbit）的通信卫星大概要花 5 亿美元，大小跟一辆校车差不多，重得跟一头大象一样。

turns.en: That's what the world's been relying upon for the past few decades for communication satellites. We've gotten now down to the point where you can create a satellite the size of a toaster.
turns.zh: 过去几十年，全世界靠的就是这种通信卫星。现在已经做到了可以造出一颗烤面包机那么大的卫星。

turns.en: And they don't cost $500 million, they cost $100,000. And that price is coming down even further. I'd say the advancements in the satellite, so for the past decade, has really enabled all new opportunities, new businesses to come about, because the cost and the size factor is creating new industries and new businesses.
turns.zh: 它们不再值 5 亿美元，只要 10 万美元，而且价格还在进一步下探。我可以说，过去十年卫星上的进步，真正催生出了全新的机会、全新的业务——成本和尺寸这两个因素正在创造出新的行业和新的公司。

turns.en: And the third is demand. The governments around the world just increasingly view space as a national strategic priority. The United States created its first new armed national service since 1947 with the U.S. Space Force back in 2019.
turns.zh: 第三是需求。世界各国政府越来越把太空视为国家层面的战略优先项。美国在 2019 年成立了美国太空军（U.S. Space Force），这是自 1947 年以来第一支新增的武装军种。

turns.en: But this is a critical new piece of national defense. It's going to be about 5% of the defense budget next year, so the U.S. government's pumping a lot of money into the U.S. Space Force for obvious reasons, military communications, surveillance, and any missile detection.
turns.zh: 但这是国防的一块全新的关键领域。明年它大概会占到国防预算的 5%，所以美国政府正往太空军里砸一大笔钱——原因很直观：军事通信、监视和导弹预警。

turns.en: And so it kind of starts there with the extent to which the government is really leaning in on space. And then there's commercial opportunities, too.
turns.zh: 所以这一切的起点，是政府有多大力度在向太空倾斜。除此之外，商业机会也在同时展开。

turns.en: Again, those flights from San Francisco to New York. Hopefully you get the internet on that plane. To me, it works 50% of the time, but that's the hope that you can get the internet to work as you're flying for five hours.
turns.zh: 还是那趟从旧金山到纽约的航班。你希望在这架飞机上能连上网络。对我来说，它有一半时间是能用的，但你的期盼就是能在那五个小时的飞行里让网络一直保持工作。

turns.en: One of the things Oscar, I'm super excited for, is direct-to-device cellular communications. And what this basically means is when you land at Newark, your phone works because it's connected to a satellite, not to a cell tower.
turns.zh: 有一件事 Oscar，是我特别兴奋的——就是终端直连卫星（direct-to-device）的蜂窝通信。它的含义基本是，当你降落在 Newark 时，你的手机能正常工作，因为它连接的是卫星，而不是基站。

turns.en: And to me, it feels like, again, half the time my phone's not working. It doesn't matter where you are in America, unless you're in a major city these days, the phone signals very spotty.
turns.zh: 在我看，说实话，我手机有一半时间是没信号的。在美国，除非你在大城市，否则手机信号非常不稳定。

turns.en: And so the promise is we're going to be able to get our phone signals from satellites, like satellite radio. It just works. I mentioned these small toaster-sized satellites.
turns.zh: 而这份承诺意味着，我们将能从卫星上获取手机信号，就像卫星广播一样——它就是好用。我前面说到这些烤面包机大小的卫星。

turns.en: There's companies like Planet Labs, they're designing these around the Earth, mapping every square inch of the Earth every day. And for areas where there's particular interest, either for commercial or military reasons, they can take a same picture of that spot ten times a day.
turns.zh: 有像 Planet Labs 这样的公司，正在绕地球部署卫星，每天把地球每一平方英寸都测绘一遍。而对某些特别关注的区域，不管是商业原因还是军事原因，他们对同一地点一天可以拍十张照片。

turns.en: It's because the satellites have gone from the size of trucks down to the size of a toaster. It's a flywheel, by the way. As more of this money from the government's being spent in the space industry, it's almost acting like venture capital, where you're creating innovations, you're reducing that cost to orbit, smaller satellites.
turns.zh: 这正是因为卫星从卡车大小做到了烤面包机大小。顺便说一句，这是一个飞轮（flywheel）：政府投入太空行业的钱越多，它就越像风险投资，你在推动创新、在压低入轨成本、把卫星做得更小。

turns.en: It's creating new businesses, new industries. Super interesting time. I think you've framed it really nicely in terms of there's two C's and a D.
turns.zh: 它在催生新的业务、新的行业。一个非常激动人心的时代。我觉得你把框架讲得非常好——两个 C 加一个 D。

turns.en: And the first C, the cost of taking mass to space has gone from 54,000 a kilogram to 3,000 a kilogram. I thought, well, that's a massive move already.
turns.zh: 第一个 C，把质量送入太空的成本，从每公斤 54,000 美元降到了 3,000 美元。我当时想，哇，这已经是一个巨大的变化了。

turns.en: But you said it's potentially going even lower than that. And certainly cost as an input for any economic decision is going to have a big impact on whether the space economy becomes more relevant.
turns.zh: 但你提到可能还会更低。而成本作为任何经济决策的投入项，一定会极大影响太空经济是否会变得更重要。

turns.en: Let's talk about artificial intelligence, which is one of those forces that is helping space to have its moment. And you've alluded to data centers in space.
turns.zh: 我们聊聊人工智能吧，它就是助推太空迎来'高光时刻'的一股力量。你之前提到过太空数据中心。

turns.en: We've talked a lot about artificial intelligence and the impact that it's having on industries here on planet Earth. But maybe talk more about why the space economy is interconnected to the artificial intelligence build out.
turns.zh: 我们聊过很多关于 AI 以及它对地球之上各行各业的影响。但也许可以再展开讲讲，为什么太空经济和 AI 基础设施建设是彼此交织的。

turns.en: Great question, Oscar, because what's happening is AI is making space more valuable and then space is going to make AI more scalable. What AI really wants is data.
turns.zh: 问得好，Oscar，因为正在发生的事情是：AI 让太空变得更有价值，而太空又会让 AI 变得更容易规模化。AI 真正想要的是数据。

turns.en: You want to train your models with the most data possible. As I mentioned before, there's companies who are literally photographing the Earth every square inch every day, creating tons of data. That was just the data repository years ago and now you can use AI. If you're a hedge fund, you're an insurance company, you're an agriculture company, you're a government that wants to look at deforestation, there's so much
turns.zh: 你希望用尽可能多的数据来训练你的模型。就像我前面提到的，有些公司简直每天把地球每一平方英寸都拍下来，产生海量数据。这在几年前还只是一个数据仓库，而现在你可以用上 AI。如果你是对冲基金、保险公司、农业公司，或者一个想研究森林砍伐的政府，有非常多

turns.en: ways you can use that data now and apply AI to it to create a lot of value. So AI is making this data from space incrementally more valuable.
turns.zh: 方式使用这些数据、把 AI 应用上去创造大量价值。所以 AI 正在让来自太空的数据在边际上变得更有价值。

turns.en: But then space is going to make AI more scalable and what I mean by that is the problem with AI on Earth right now is the need for power and the need for land and the need for water and the need for governments to cooperate and the need for U.S. citizens and global citizens to cooperate, building data centers in their backyards. These are problems. There's a lot of problems and a slowdown potentially
turns.zh: 而太空会让 AI 更容易规模化。我指的是，眼下地球上 AI 面临的问题是需要电力、需要土地、需要水，需要政府配合，需要美国民众和全球民众配合、在自己家后院建数据中心。这些都是问题，有很多问题，也可能带来一场放缓——

turns.en: of can we build a data center capacity we need due to all these pending issues. For some of these issues, orbits, the Earth orbit is where to put a data center because you're not dealing with governments or neighbors, you've got power or you got cooling. This is the vision that the data centers that we currently see being built out in Texas and in Europe and in Virginia next decade will start to see the incremental
turns.zh: 我们究竟能不能建出所需的数据中心容量，取决于所有这些悬而未决的问题。对其中一些问题来说，轨道——地球轨道——正是放置数据中心的地方，因为你不用再和政府或邻居打交道，你有电力，也有冷却。这就是那个愿景：我们目前看到在德克萨斯、在欧洲、在弗吉尼亚建的那些数据中心，在下一个十年，边际

turns.en: capacity going into orbit. So it's amazing time right now. It would sound pretty complicated to launch a data center into space and that presumably it should be easier to solve for that on Earth. But as you're pointing out, there's a lot of stakeholders involved in getting that data center approved in terms of land and where to put it.
turns.zh: 新增容量将会走向轨道。所以，真是令人惊叹的时刻。听上去把一座数据中心送上太空应该非常复杂，按理说在地球上解决这个问题应该更容易。但正如你所指出的，要让一座数据中心获批，涉及太多利益相关方——土地、选址等等。

turns.en: And I'm thinking a little bit about the BII mid-year outlook. When we talk to Jean Bovon, one of the big themes of that outlook is this theme of scarcity versus abundance and the scarcity point has to do with the scarcity of natural resources and other materials and minerals that are required in terms of building a data center. Is there anything else you would point to that is an interesting contrast between the difficulty
turns.zh: 我在想 BII（BlackRock 投资研究所）的年中展望。当我们和 Jean Boivin 交流时，那份展望里一个大主题就是稀缺与丰裕的对比。稀缺那一侧说的是建造数据中心所必需的自然资源、材料和矿产的稀缺。除了这些，你还会指出什么有意思的对比——

turns.en: of building the data center on Earth versus launching it into space? Really it's about time to power. That's what the AI companies are primarily concerned about.
turns.zh: 在地球上建造数据中心与把它送入太空之间的难度对比？说到底就是'接电时间'（time to power）。这才是 AI 公司最关心的。

turns.en: That simple sentence, time to power. The chips are becoming much more abundant. Factories around the world are pumping out the components and whatever shortages we see in 2026 gets resolved over time.
turns.zh: 就这么简单的一句话——接电时间。芯片正在变得越来越充裕，全球各地的工厂在量产这些零部件，无论 2026 年出现什么短缺，都会随着时间被解决。

turns.en: But this time to power issue is the problem. The U.S. grid, frankly global energy grids, were not designed to provide power the speed at which companies would love to expand their AI compute capacity. So time to power, that's the problem. The other problem is capital. So if you think about what's happening with the construction of a data center, it costs about 50 billion dollars to create one gigawatt of AI
turns.zh: 但真正的问题是这个接电时间。坦白讲，美国电网——甚至可以说是全球能源电网——在设计之初就没有考虑过要让电力跟上公司扩张 AI 算力的速度。所以接电时间才是那个问题。第二个问题是资本。你想一下，建造一座数据中心，产生一吉瓦（gigawatt）的 AI 算力大约要花 500 亿美元。

turns.en: compute. And if you break down the 50 billion, that's about 30 billion dollars of compute IT infrastructure and then about 20 billion dollars of everything else. The power, the cooling, the land, the shell, the labor.
turns.zh: 把这 500 亿拆开来看，大约 300 亿美元是算力 IT 基础设施，另外大约 200 亿美元是所有其他东西——电力、冷却、土地、外壳、人工。

turns.en: So it's not just an issue of can we get the power, it's also can we build these more efficiently and cheaply. And as you bring down the cost curve of getting that one gigawatt of compute live, your returns go up. So there's an incentive to reduce the cost, reduce the 50 billion.
turns.zh: 所以这不仅是能不能拿到电的问题，也是我们能不能更高效、更便宜地把它们建起来。当你把这一吉瓦算力的成本曲线打下来，你的回报就上去了。所以这里有强烈的动机去压成本、去把这 500 亿降下来。

turns.en: And if you think about, if we can put a gigawatt of AI compute in space, primarily you're attacking that 20 billion dollar piece. The compute stays the same, the compute costs, but the power piece that gets reduced because you go from relying on a grid or turbines or fuel cells to solar panels. And by the way, the solar generation in space is about five times more efficient than on Earth.
turns.zh: 你想想看——如果我们能把一吉瓦的 AI 算力放到太空里，你主要攻的就是那 200 亿美元这一块。算力部分不变、算力成本不变，但电力部分会显著下降，因为你不再依赖电网、燃气轮机或燃料电池，而是转向太阳能板。顺便说一下，太空中的太阳能发电效率大约是地球上的 5 倍。

turns.en: Solar to power AI compute makes a ton of sense. Cooling, cooling is a major problem Oscar for data centers. Literally they have to build these tunnels and liquid cool and this is a very big architectural problem to think about how do you build a future data center. But there's no problem in space with cooling because you use the vacuum of space to cool those chips.
turns.zh: 用太阳能来给 AI 算力供电，逻辑非常通。冷却——Oscar，冷却对数据中心来说是一个大问题——他们简直得挖这些隧道、做液冷，这是一个非常庞大的建筑难题：未来的数据中心到底怎么建。但在太空里没有冷却的问题，你可以用太空的真空来给那些芯片降温。

turns.en: Seems like it's crazy to put a server with some envidia chips on into orbit, but it actually makes all the sense in the world. And where there's an economic incentive to do something, people will figure it out.
turns.zh: 把一台装了 Nvidia 芯片的服务器放到轨道上，听起来很疯狂，但其实完全说得通。而只要一件事存在经济激励，人们就会想办法把它做出来。

turns.en: So from a timing perspective, there's going to be the first real demonstration of this concept of a server running AI compute in space, probably Q4 of 2027, that SpaceX's target timeline to show us that first proof of concept with scale in 2028 clearly, but that'll be the first time we'll see that first demonstration of a server in space.
turns.zh: 所以从时间线看，这个概念——一台服务器在太空跑 AI 算力——的首次真正演示，大概是 2027 年四季度；SpaceX 的目标时间线是在 2028 年展示具备规模的首个概念验证。很明显，那将是我们第一次看到太空服务器的演示。

turns.en: Right, as you're talking about this, it all sounds so futuristic and conceptual, but now you're putting some dates around when we will actually see some of this in practice and those dates are really not too far in the future.
turns.zh: 对，你一边讲，一切听起来都那么未来、那么概念化，但你现在给出了具体的时间点，而且这些时间点其实离现在并不遥远。

turns.en: Reid, when we talked about why space is having its moment right now or why it's rising in relevance, you touched on national security and defense spending and the role that governments play. We actually spoke to your colleague, Ralph Heitmeier, about this topic of defense investing and how governments are spending more time here. Can you talk about the importance of space to national security again and where do government
turns.zh: Reid，我们谈到为什么太空正在迎来它的时刻、为什么重要性在上升时，你提到了国家安全和国防开支、政府扮演的角色。我们之前其实和你的同事 Ralph Heitmeier 聊过国防投资这个话题，聊到各国政府正在这里投入更多精力。你能再讲讲太空对国家安全的重要性吗——以及政府

turns.en: priorities intersect with some of the commercial priorities that technology companies might have? Sure, what's been really interesting to watch over the past few years is space is becoming as important to control as the land and sea. This is modern warfare.
turns.zh: 的优先事项和科技公司可能有的商业优先事项，在哪儿交汇？可以。过去几年特别值得关注的现象是：太空已经变得和陆地、海洋一样，成为各方争夺控制权的关键领域。这就是现代战争。

turns.en: Governments want satellites for secure communications and for surveillance, but there's increasingly a view of you need to control space and there's concerns, frankly, about potential foreign adversaries targeting satellites in space. Those GPS satellites I mentioned earlier, how vulnerable are they?
turns.zh: 政府需要卫星，用于安全通信和监视，但越来越多的观点是：你必须控制太空，坦白说，大家也在担心潜在的外国对手在轨上瞄准卫星。我前面说到的那些 GPS 卫星，它们到底有多脆弱？

turns.en: There's only 30 of them and so the inability to keep those in the air would be devastating. This is why the US Space Force was created. This is why the budget's going up 100% next year because the US government, frankly, feels this way.
turns.zh: 总共只有 30 颗，所以如果无法让它们继续在空中运转，后果将是毁灭性的。这正是为什么成立了美国太空军，这也是为什么明年它的预算要翻一倍——因为美国政府坦白讲就是这么想的。

turns.en: You need to control space. This is modern warfare. This is the new Star Wars in orbit. You mentioned the marriage of these two worlds. This money that's going in from the government into the commercial space industry was really funding the R&D. Better rockets, better satellites, better communication equipment and so it's a very symbiotic relationship where it's bringing down the costs of the private sector
turns.zh: 你必须控制太空。这是现代战争，这是轨道上的新'星球大战'。你提到了这两个世界的联姻——政府投入到商业太空行业的这笔钱，实际上是在为研发买单：更好的火箭、更好的卫星、更好的通信设备，所以这是一种非常共生的关系，一边压低私营部门的成本，

turns.en: at the same time the governments around the world are benefiting from better optimized space infrastructure. And so Reid, if we think about the space economy as a bit of an ecosystem from rockets launching into space satellites, we're talking about the different component parts and infrastructure that are required. You mentioned data centers.
turns.zh: 另一边全世界政府也从更优化的太空基础设施中受益。Reid，如果把太空经济当作一个生态系统来想——从发射入轨的火箭、卫星，我们谈到各种必要的组成部分和基础设施——你提到了数据中心。

turns.en: You see the most significant areas of economic opportunity emerging today and how does that opportunity set change over time? Very simply I would just start with the picks and shovels. All of these satellites take semiconductors.
turns.zh: 你看到的最重要的经济机会在哪儿？这些机会的格局随时间又会怎么变？非常简单，我会先从'镐头和铁锹'（picks and shovels）说起。所有这些卫星都要用半导体。

turns.en: They take communication equipment, lasers rocket componentry, specialty materials they need to have materials that can withstand high heat levels. I would then next talk about the services. What are we going to see emerge if more stuff gets into orbit? What does that enable? And I mentioned earlier this concept of new industries that can form when you've got very cheap form factors getting to space
turns.zh: 它们要用通信设备、激光器、火箭零部件、特种材料——需要能承受高温的材料。接下来我会讲服务。如果更多东西进入轨道，我们会看到什么浮现出来？这会解锁什么？我前面提到过一个概念：当以极低的成本把设备送入太空时，新的行业就会形成——

turns.en: cheaply. This earth observation but weather mapping any value of having images of the earth is all sorts of industries that would love to get access to that data. The services that are going to emerge are going to be very interesting businesses and not to mention the companies that have to service just the space economy. So there's going to be a lot of orbital debris. We're going to have to clean that up. Things we're not even thinking about
turns.zh: 地球观测、天气制图——拥有地球影像的价值，会有各种行业都想要访问这些数据。将会浮现出来的服务，本身就是非常有趣的生意。更不用提那些只是给太空经济本身提供服务的公司。会有大量轨道碎片（orbital debris），我们得把它清理掉。还有一些我们现在甚至还没开始想的东西——

turns.en: right now Oscar and then of course the data center and space topic. It's highly profound to think about next decade if all the compute capacity for AI training goes into orbit, how does that change the outlook for the magnificent seven?
turns.zh: Oscar——然后当然就是太空数据中心这个话题。值得深思的是：如果未来十年所有用于 AI 训练的算力都进入轨道，那会怎么改变对'Magnificent 7'（七巨头）的前景判断？

turns.en: How does that change the outlook for the major frontier labs? Who's got a play right now in space? Who's making the moves right now in the year 2026 to ensure that they've got access to space?
turns.zh: 会怎么改变对主要前沿实验室（frontier labs）的前景判断？现在谁在太空里有布局？谁正在 2026 年动手做那些事，以确保自己能拿到进入太空的入场券？

turns.en: There's very few companies by the way. It's one of things I'm watching very keenly is which companies are making the right moves right now to be positioned if this data center and space concept is where the incremental computers next decade, who gets left behind and who's very well positioned for that?
turns.zh: 顺便说，这样的公司其实非常少。我最近特别关注的一件事，就是哪些公司正在做正确的动作，以便如果'太空数据中心'真的承接了下个十年的边际算力，谁会被落下、谁会被非常好地卡位。

turns.en: Right. It sounds like there's a more immediate and perhaps more obvious investment opportunity set that you can look at. You mentioned the picks and shovels, the materials, the component parts, the semis, but the second and third order effects are less known right now, but something that will evolve over time in an area that you can monitor and that investors can take advantage of. And so speaking of investors, I think if they're listening
turns.zh: 对，听起来有一批更贴近当下、也更直观的投资机会可以去关注——你提到了'镐头和铁锹'、材料、零部件、半导体。但二阶和三阶效应目前还不那么为人所知，是随时间演化的，也是你可以持续跟踪、投资者能从中获益的一个领域。说到投资者——我觉得如果现在有投资者在听

turns.en: to this read, they're perhaps still trying to wrap their mind around this evolving economy that is going on in space and maybe they think it sounds a little bit like science fiction, which I wouldn't blame them, but what do you think they may be missing?
turns.zh: 这一集，他们可能还在消化这个正在太空中成型的新经济，可能觉得它多少有点像科幻小说——我也不怪他们这么想——但你觉得他们可能漏掉了什么？

turns.en: And on the other side of that, what are the risks or uncertainties they're right to be cautious about? It's a great question, Oscar, because I would just go back to the two C's that we started with, cost and capability.
turns.zh: 反过来讲，又有哪些风险或不确定性，是他们保持谨慎是有道理的？问得好，Oscar，我想还是回到我们一开始说的那两个 C——成本和能力。

turns.en: Investors or anybody listening in this podcast should not underestimate what happens when the cost of a kilogram of mass to orbit goes from $54,000 to $200.
turns.zh: 投资者或者任何在听这档播客的人，都不应该低估当一公斤质量入轨的成本从 54,000 美元降到 200 美元时会发生什么。

turns.en: And the satellite that goes to orbit is not the size of a school bus with the wingspan of a 737 but it's the size of a toaster. That's the structural change that is enabling what we're seeing right now with the space economy in the year 2026. The risks, however, are enormous. I've talked to executives Oscar that have tried to downplay space.
turns.zh: 而当入轨的卫星不再是那架翼展堪比 737 客机的'校车'，而只是一台烤面包机——这就是正在支撑我们看到 2026 年太空经济的结构性变化。但风险同样巨大。我接触过一些高管，Oscar，他们试图淡化太空。

turns.en: What I have learned looking at the space now for about a decade is that space is really hard, meaning the risk profile of space companies are higher than you think. In other words, the world's wealthiest, smartest people right now are trying to figure this out with varying levels of success.
turns.zh: 过去十年我观察太空学到的一件事是：太空真的非常难。也就是说，太空公司的风险水平比你想的要高。换句话说，世界上最富有、最聪明的一群人现在都在琢磨这件事，成功与否参差不齐。

turns.en: Some companies are getting to orbit, some companies are blowing up with a launchpad as we speak. These are the world's smartest minds with endless capital.
turns.zh: 有些公司做到了入轨，有些公司就在我们说话的当口在发射台上炸了。这些都是世界上最聪明的大脑，带着无限的资本。

turns.en: So space is really hard. I remember one executive telling me, oh no, it's okay. Araka is nothing more than a tin can with a fuse at the end. And that company never got to orbit.
turns.zh: 所以太空真的很难。我记得有位高管跟我说：'没事，Astra 不过就是一个尾巴上绑了根导火索的锡罐。'结果那家公司始终没能入轨。

turns.en: I eagerly watched the SpaceX launches which they now live streamed to see how they're doing. I look at the competitors but I would just leave you with space is hard.
turns.zh: 我一直在密切关注 SpaceX 的发射，他们现在都是直播的——就想看看他们进展如何。我也在看其他竞争对手。我只想给你留一句：太空很难。

turns.en: All this sounds, you're right, science fiction. And to get to the actual movie where there's a happy ending to take a lot of hard work and a lot of failure along the way. Right. Execution is difficult.
turns.zh: 这一切——你说得对——听着像科幻。要拍到那部有 Happy Ending 的电影，需要一路的艰辛和大量的失败。对，执行本身极其困难。

turns.en: Like you said, there's a lot of smart people trying to do this and it makes the role of an investor perhaps really important here to identify the correct opportunities.
turns.zh: 正如你所说，有很多聪明人在做这件事，这也让投资人的角色在这里可能变得格外重要——去识别出正确的机会。

turns.en: Reed, if we were to fast forward and let's say we're having this conversation again 10 years from now, which at the rate things are changing, I can only imagine what 10 years is going to look like. But if we were having that conversation, what developments in the space economy do you think would make your expectations today look conservative? And what should we be watching between now and then?
turns.zh: Reid，如果我们快进十年——假设 10 年后我们再来聊同样的话题。以事情变化的速度，我根本无法想象十年后是什么样。但如果我们那时再聊，你觉得太空经济的哪些进展会让你今天的预期显得保守？从现在到那时，我们应该关注什么？

turns.en: Yeah, Oscar, it's going to come down to how quickly can the industry come down that cost curve of getting mass to orbit. We're going to start there. If it's faster than expected, we're going to have a much larger space economy. If it's slower because the reusability of the rockets are more challenging than expected, the space economy gets pushed out. So we'll start there at the pace at which this happens
turns.zh: 是的，Oscar，说到底还是要看这个行业能多快把质量入轨的成本曲线打下来。我们从这里开始。如果比预期更快，我们就会看到一个规模大得多的太空经济；如果因为火箭可复用比预想更具挑战、进展更慢，太空经济就会被推后。所以我们先看节奏——

turns.en: that they can bring down the cost curve. The second piece would be just watching where is incremental AI compute built next decade. Are we still building in Texas in the year 2031?
turns.zh: 他们把成本曲线打下来的速度。第二件事，就是看下一个十年的边际 AI 算力建在哪儿。到 2031 年我们还在德克萨斯建吗？

turns.en: Or is it an orbit? Based on those two answers is going to be dependent or is going to drive, I should say, the success of what this industry is building towards. To me, Oscar Space feels like the early days of the Internet where somebody had the concept, what if we just network people together? Wouldn't that be a great idea? That was the Internet. And that got built. But nobody could have foreseen the
turns.zh: 还是在轨道上？行业最终能否成功，取决于——更准确地说，是被——这两个答案所驱动。对我来说，Oscar，太空感觉就像互联网早期：有人提出了一个概念，'如果我们把人们都联网，会不会很棒？'那就是互联网。它被建起来了，但没人能预料到

turns.en: smartphone, social networking, cloud computing, all these things that came out of the basic concept of just connect people, network the world. You created arguably today's largest companies and industries from that simple ideas. I think about the next decade, the mid-2030s is who are the new trillion dollar companies that are leveraging the ability to get to space cheaply and reliably.
turns.zh: 智能手机、社交网络、云计算——这些全都源自'连接人们、让世界联网'这一个简单的概念。正是从这个简单的想法里，造就了今天全球最大的公司和行业。我在想未来十年、2030 年代中期，会是哪些新的万亿美元级公司——那些正在利用'便宜而可靠地进入太空'能力的公司。

turns.en: It's going to be an amazing decade. It does feel like some new movies are going to come out of these next five or ten years as the space economy evolves.
turns.zh: 这将会是了不起的十年。确实感觉，随着太空经济演化，未来五到十年还会诞生几部新的电影级别的故事。

turns.en: Reid, you said a lot of interesting things and I was just thinking back to some of the things you said. You said mass to orbit and the cost of that.
turns.zh: Reid，你讲了很多有意思的东西，我回想了一下你说的内容。你提到质量入轨，以及那背后的成本。

turns.en: You mentioned time to power and the importance that plays for the builder of a data center. You mentioned two C's and a D, which is a good framework to think about why the space economy is becoming more relevant. I can confirm that you and I had this conversation when we were talking about space, but at this rate, in ten years, we might be in space and instead talking about the economy back on Earth.
turns.zh: 你提到接电时间，以及它对数据中心建造方的重要性。你提到两个 C 加一个 D——这是一个很好的框架，用来理解为什么太空经济正变得越来越重要。我可以确认，你和我确实聊过太空这个话题。但按这个速度，十年后，我们可能自己就在太空里了，反过来聊地球上的经济。

turns.en: I'll check in with you and see if that prediction comes true. Reid, thanks for sharing all these insights and thanks for doing it here on The Bid. Thanks, Oscar.
